## Objectives

- See what a principal component *is*: a direction, not a variable
- Read loadings, scores, and the scree plot — and stop at the right number
- Find the **latent drivers** behind twenty questionnaire items
- Meet the idea that comes back in week 5: compression as a model

## Why a manager cares

::: {.subtitle-frame}
Twenty questions, three answers
:::

- A customer satisfaction survey has 24 items. The board wants to know *what drives satisfaction*. Not 24 things — two or three.
- A hospital collects 30 quality indicators per ward. They move together in ways nobody can see in a spreadsheet.
- Before a churn model, 80 behavioural columns — many of them near-copies of each other

In each case the data are **wide** and **redundant**. PCA finds the few directions along which they actually vary, and throws away the rest.

## [Section 1]{.section-kicker} The idea {.section-slide background-color="#002f57"}

## A component is a direction

::: {.subtitle-frame}
Stated without matrices first
:::

Picture the data as a cloud of $n$ points in $p$ dimensions.

- The **first principal component** is the line through the cloud along which the points are *most spread out*
- The **second** is the line at right angles to the first with the most remaining spread
- And so on, $p$ times — but the spread runs out fast

Each point's **score** is its coordinate along that line. Each variable's **loading** is how much it contributes to the direction.

::: {.callout-note}
Nothing is dropped, yet. PCA is a *rotation*. Compression happens when you keep the first few components and discard the others — and you decide how many.
:::

## The direction, found by looking for it

{{< video media/Rotation.mp4 width="1000" height="562" >}}

A line turns through the cloud while the variance of the projection is measured at every angle. It stops where that number is largest. The first component is not a metaphor about spread — it is the argument of a maximum, and this is that maximum being found.

## The same thing, in one line

For centred data $X$ ($n \times p$), the first component is the unit vector $\phi_1$ that maximises the variance of the projection:

$$
\phi_1 = \arg\max_{\lVert \phi \rVert = 1} \; \operatorname{Var}(X \phi)
$$

- The solution is the leading **eigenvector of the covariance matrix** $X^\top X / n$
- Its eigenvalue $\lambda_1$ is the variance it captures. $\lambda_1 / \sum_j \lambda_j$ is the *proportion of variance explained*
- Components 2, 3, … are the next eigenvectors, orthogonal to the previous ones

Everything you will read off a PCA is one of: a loading vector $\phi_k$, a score $X\phi_k$, or a variance share $\lambda_k / \sum \lambda$.

## By hand: two variables, perfectly correlated

Height and arm span, standardised, for four people: $(-1.5,-1.5), (-0.5,-0.5), (0.5,0.5), (1.5,1.5)$.

- The cloud is a line at 45°. The first component is that line: $\phi_1 = (0.71, 0.71)$
- Scores along it: $-2.1, -0.7, 0.7, 2.1$. Variance $= 2.5$
- The second component is perpendicular: $\phi_2 = (0.71, -0.71)$. Every score is $0$. Variance $= 0$.

**Two variables, one component, 100% of the variance.** You had two columns and one piece of information. That is the whole method, in the simplest case it can be seen in.

## By hand, watched

{{< video media/PCAByHand.mp4 width="1000" height="562" >}}

Four people, every score computed, and a second component whose variance is exactly zero. When two columns say the same thing, PCA says so with a number.

## Scale, again

PCA is a variance-hunter. A variable measured in thousands *is* the first component, whatever it means.

- **Standardise** — `scale. = TRUE` — unless every column is already in the same unit and you *want* the large-variance ones to dominate
- On a survey where every item is 1–5, you may leave it; on customer behaviour, you may not

::: {.callout-important title="Attention"}
Same trap as clustering, same fix, same reason. Distance and variance are both blind to units.
:::

## [Section 2]{.section-kicker} How many, and what do they mean {.section-slide background-color="#002f57"}

## How many components to keep

- **Scree plot**: variance explained per component. Keep the ones before the curve flattens — the *elbow*, again
- **Cumulative share**: keep enough to reach 70–80% — a convention, not a law
- **Kaiser**: keep components with eigenvalue $> 1$ on standardised data, i.e. that explain more than one original variable's worth

They disagree often. When they do, prefer the smaller number you can **interpret**. A component nobody can name is not a driver; it is noise with a label.

## Three rules, three answers

{{< video media/ScreeChoice.mp4 width="1000" height="562" >}}

The same scree plot under the three rules you were just given. They disagree, and no amount of staring resolves it. The choice is yours to make and yours to defend — which is why the exercise asks for the sentence, not the number.

## Naming a component

Read its loadings. Large positive and large negative loadings tell you what the direction *contrasts*.

| Item | PC1 | PC2 |
|---|---|---|
| Staff courtesy | **0.48** | 0.05 |
| Waiting time | **0.45** | −0.10 |
| Clarity of explanations | **0.47** | 0.02 |
| Price fairness | 0.08 | **0.71** |
| Value for money | 0.11 | **0.68** |

PC1: *service experience*. PC2: *price perception*. Two drivers, from five items — and now a regression of satisfaction on **two** scores instead of five collinear columns.

## In R

```{.r code-line-numbers="1-2|4|6-7|9-10|12"}
library(tidyverse); library(factoextra)
X <- USArrests                                  # 50 states, 4 crime rates + urban pop

pca <- prcomp(X, scale. = TRUE)

summary(pca)                                    # variance explained, cumulative
fviz_eig(pca)                                   # scree

pca$rotation                                    # loadings: variable × component
head(pca$x)                                     # scores: state × component

fviz_pca_biplot(pca, repel = TRUE)              # both at once — the plot to show
```

::: {.callout-note}
On `USArrests`, PC1 loads on all three violent-crime rates: *overall crime*. PC2 is urban population alone: *urbanisation*. Two components, 87% of the variance, and both have a name.
:::

## The biplot, read properly

- **Points** are observations, placed by their scores on PC1 and PC2
- **Arrows** are variables, drawn from their loadings
- A long arrow: the variable is well represented in these two components
- Two arrows at a small angle: the variables are correlated. At 90°: not. Opposite: negatively.
- A point far out along an arrow scores high on that variable

It is the single most information-dense plot in this course. Spend the lab learning to read one.

## [Section 3]{.section-kicker} Compression as a model {.section-slide background-color="#002f57"}

## PCA reconstructs

Keep $q < p$ components. From the scores you can *rebuild* an approximation of every row:

$$
\hat X \;=\; (X \Phi_q)\, \Phi_q^\top
$$

- $q = p$: perfect reconstruction. $q = 1$: each row is replaced by its projection on one line
- The reconstruction error $\lVert X - \hat X \rVert^2$ is exactly the variance you threw away

::: {.callout-note}
Hold this thought for week 5. A neural network that learns to compress its input to $q$ numbers and rebuild it is called an **autoencoder** — and with linear activations, it *is* PCA. Nonlinear activations make it a PCA that can bend.
:::

## A component is what your variables have in common. Naming it is your job, not the algorithm's.  {.statement}
